title: Waring's g(2) = 4 as a Sharp, Axiom-Free Least Element
content: The header contrasts this entry with its parent umbrella, which stated Waring's theorem for squares only as the conjunction '4 suffices and 7 needs 4' and was tagged `axiomatized` because it evaluated worked examples with `native_decide` (trusting `Lean.ofReduceBool`). Here the result is stated sharply: defining `Sufficient k` = 'every natural is a sum of k squares', the *least* such k — Waring's g(2) — is exactly 4, packaged as both `IsLeast` and `sInf = 4`. The upper bound is Lagrange's four-square theorem; the lower bound is the mod-8 obstruction at 7. Everything stays inside `decide`/`omega`, so the file is genuinely 0-axiom. Single import `Mathlib` brings `Nat.sum_four_squares`, `ZMod`, `Fin.snoc`, and `IsLeast`/`sInf`.
mathContext: $g(2) = \min\{k : \forall n,\ n = \textstyle\sum_{i<k} x_i^2\} = 4.$ The lower bound is witnessed by $7$, and more generally by the forms $4^a(8b+7)$ (Legendre/Gauss three-square theorem).

title: Representability and Its Monotonicity in k
content: `IsSumOfSquares k n` is defined as the existence of a tuple $f : \mathrm{Fin}\,k \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\sum_i (f i)^2 = n$. The key structural fact is monotonicity: `IsSumOfSquares.succ` pads a $k$-square representation with one zero square (`Fin.snoc f 0`, then `Fin.sum_univ_castSucc` to peel the last entry), and `IsSumOfSquares.mono` iterates this by induction on the difference $l - k$. Monotonicity is exactly what makes the 'sufficient' set $\{k \mid \text{Sufficient } k\}$ upward closed, and what later promotes 'no $k \le 3$ representation of 7' into the sharp lower bound $4 \le k$.
mathContext: $n = \sum_{i<k} x_i^2 \Rightarrow n = \sum_{i<k} x_i^2 + 0^2 = \sum_{i<k+1} x_i'^2$. Hence $k \le l$ and IsSumOfSquares $k$ $n$ ⟹ IsSumOfSquares $l$ $n$.

title: Upper Bound (Lagrange) and the Sharp Mod-8 Obstruction
content: `four_squares_universal` is the upper bound $4 \in \{k \mid \text{Sufficient}\}$: it wraps Mathlib's `Nat.sum_four_squares` into the `IsSumOfSquares 4` shape via the explicit 4-tuple `![a,b,c,d]` and `Fin.sum_univ_four`. `seven_not_three` is the sharp lower-bound witness: 7 is not a sum of three squares. The proof casts the hypothetical equation $x^2+y^2+z^2 = 7$ into $\mathrm{ZMod}\,8$ and finishes with a finite `decide` check that no three elements of $\{0,1,4\}$ (the squares mod 8) sum to 7. Using `decide` (kernel reduction) rather than `native_decide` is what keeps the whole development 0-axiom.
mathContext: Squares mod 8 are $\{0, 1, 4\}$; the 27 ordered triples are checked exhaustively and none gives $a^2+b^2+c^2 \equiv 7 \pmod 8$. So $7 \ne x^2+y^2+z^2$ over $\mathbb{N}$.

title: g(2) = 4 as IsLeast and as an Infimum
content: `Sufficient k` collects the square-counts that represent every natural. `g2_isLeast` proves `IsLeast {k | Sufficient k} 4`: membership is `four_squares_universal`, and the lower-bound half assumes some sufficient $k$ and derives a contradiction if $k < 4$ — then $k \le 3$, so the (assumed) representation of 7 promotes via `IsSumOfSquares.mono` to a 3-square representation, contradicting `seven_not_three`. `waring_g2` converts the least element to the infimum form $\sInf\{k \mid \text{Sufficient } k\} = 4$ via `IsLeast.csInf_eq`. The closing `four_squares_suffice` / `three_squares_insufficient` give the human-readable two halves.
mathContext: $\mathrm{IsLeast}\,S\,4 \iff 4 \in S \land \forall k \in S,\ 4 \le k$. With $S = \{k \mid \text{Sufficient } k\}$: $4 \in S$ (Lagrange) and any $k \in S$ has $k \ge 4$ (else 7 fails), so $g(2) = \min S = \sInf S = 4$.
